    Sprint 5 – Deployment, Optimization and Reliability

    📄

    Deployment architecture patterns for AI Systems

    Lesson 1

    Shipping an LLM application is rarely blocked by models not being able to answer specific questions (there are ways to route the system such that unanswerable questions would not be processed). It is blocked by not being able to meet p95 latency, keeping costs predictable, rolling out without breaking prod and recovering fast when prompt templates are changed unintentionally. Deployment architecture is where these concerns can be tackled.

    This lesson maps the common LLM workloads to deployment patterns, then goes into the progressive delivery that is a requirement for most LLM based systems.



    Picking a Deployment Pattern to optimize for your case.


    Usually, the system you are building would face some SLOs and constraints. The choice for an architectural pattern would be tied to these. Here are some examples:


    • Latency targets - Chat UIs need sub‑second TTFT (Time To First Token) with streamed tokens. Back‑office jobs can wait minutes or hours. Think about real-time chatbot vs. a ticketing system where expected time to answer can vary from an hour to a few days.

    • Throughput and concurrency - Are you handling a small number of heavy requests or a large flow of small ones.

    • Costs - Are you on vendor APIs, self‑hosting on GPUs or a mix. Is cost per request, per token, or per job predictable enough for finance teams.

    • Workload type - Interactive chat, tool‑heavy agent flows, retrieval‑centric tasks or offline batch processing.

    • Change rate - How often do prompts and tools change. Do you need continuous delivery at the traffic layer or at the feature flag layer.


    When planning for the system design, you should keep the above close as you evaluate each pattern in the following section.



    The deployment patterns.


    Pattern 1 - Edge streaming frontend connected to a stateless API


    Interactive UX needs sub‑second time‑to‑first‑token (TTFT). The browser should see tokens as soon as the provider emits them. This is where the edge functions come in. You can achieve the lowest latency by streaming from the LLM provider to your edge function and relaying chunks to the client with Server‑Sent Events (SSE) or streamed fetch responses.


    Implementation: Browser connects to your edge function. Edge function calls your LLM provider with streaming set to true and relays tokens to the client. If your app sits behind NGINX or an ingress, you disable proxy buffering on the streaming route so chunks are flushed as they arrive. For example, OpenAI’s API sends Server‑Sent Events when stream=true. Edge runtimes like Cloudflare Workers and Vercel Edge support web streams natively. In systems like NGINX you may need proxy_buffering set to off.


    Use this when: You build chat or copilot style UX where time‑to‑first‑token is most of the perceived speed.

    SLO considerations: Best TTFT and interactive feel. Latency to model still applies, but users see progress.

    Scaling: Edge scales horizontally by POP (Point of Presence - where the edge function is hosted). 

    Cost: Cheap at the compute layer. The cost driver is tokens.


    Security considerations: Never expose provider keys to the browser. The edge function owns credentials and enforces auth.


    Pitfalls.

    • Buffered proxies break streaming. Verify NGINX and ingress settings on the exact streaming route. 

    • Region choice matters. Pin preferred regions for edge functions if you must keep traffic in specific geolocations.



    Pattern 2 - Application container with a potential sidecar


    A standard microservice approach that adds TLS, auth, rate limiting, circuit breaking and consistent logging while your app container focuses on orchestration, tool calls or RAG. Potentially use a sidecar to handle egress policy, retries and streaming pass through so that non-application level concerns stay out of app code.




    Implementation: Client -> API gateway -> app container. Sidecars handle cross‑cutting concerns: TLS, routing, circuit breaking, auth and connectivity. 


    Use this when: You want a standard microservice entry point with streaming, retries, circuit breaking and consistent logging. The app calls one or more providers, tools and vector stores.


    SLO considerations: Good for most SaaS style LLM features. Slight overhead from gateways and sidecars.


    Scaling: Horizontal scaling with HPA (Horizontal pod Autoscaler in Kubernetes) on CPU plus custom metrics like requests in flight or tokens per second.


    Cost: Predictable. Most cost is still tokens or GPU time downstream.


    Pitfalls.


    • If you stream through the gateway, confirm it passes chunked responses or SSE without buffering.



    Pattern 3 - Asynchronous workflow with queue‑based load balancing


    This pattern is all about implementing event-driven processing in your Agentic System pipeline. You can acknowledge requests fast and push work to a durable queue. Scale consumer workers on queue depth, enforce idempotency keys for all side effects, and add dead letter queues for non-processable messages. This pattern absorbs bursts, supports long running agent flows and keeps tail latency and costs predictable.




    Implementation: Front-facing API returns 202 plus a job id. The request is pushed to a durable queue (e.g. SQS, Kafka etc.). Workers pull data and apply processing. A status endpoint, webhooks, or another queue notifies completion. This is the classic queue‑based load balancing pattern.


    Use this when: Requests can be acknowledged fast and finished later. Examples: long reports, multi‑tool agent runs, heavy data extraction, or when you must survive bursts of traffic.


    SLO considerations: Great for throughput and cost smoothing. Users trade interactive latency for reliability and scale.


    Scaling: You can adjust replica count of AI Agent consumers connected to the work queue.


    Cost: You can run workers on cheap CPU nodes and pay only when the queue has work.


    Pitfalls.


    • Idempotency of the operations is a hard requirement and deduplication mechanisms should be set in place since some messages will be processed twice due to retry mechanisms.

    • Implement backoff mechanisms and dead-letter queues to not halt the entire processing pipeline.



    Pattern 4 - Batch and offline inference.


    For large backfills and periodic jobs such as summarization, labeling or re embedding, you can run batch endpoints or DAGs that read from object storage and write results back. Partition inputs into idempotent shards, use spot or preemptible nodes with checkpointing and set retry and straggler policies. Optimized for throughput and predictable completion windows rather than interactive latency.




    Implementation: You run your Agents as a part of ETL/ELT Process on a given schedule. An agent takes the form of a CLI script most of the time and is scheduled to run periodically via tools like Apache Airflow. You consume the accumulated work, connect to external context and tools if needed and save the agent's results to a batch storage. Computation results can be loaded into a real-time storage and used for real time applications as well.


    Use this when: You need to process large corpora on a schedule or at high throughput. E.g. nightly summarization, document grading, log or ticket labeling, lead enrichment, content redaction or big backfills for new prompts.


    SLO considerations: Throughput over latency. Jobs can run for minutes to hours, but you must deliver predictable completion times.


    Scaling: Use job queues and chunk inputs into partitions sized for your workers.


    Cost: Cheapest way to push huge volumes. Use spot or preemptible nodes for non‑urgent batches and checkpoint so you can resume.


    Reliability patterns.


    • Idempotent shards. Make each shard repeatable by id. Store intermediate outputs keyed by shard id.

    • At‑least‑once handling. Expect reruns after node failure or preemption.

    • Straggler mitigation. Split large shards, requeue the slow ones.



    Checklist for quickly picking the right deployment pattern.


    • Interactive chat, strong perception of speed -> Pattern 1 or 2 with streaming.

    • Burstiness or long‑running steps -> Pattern 3 with queue‑based load balancing and idempotency.

    • Nightly or backfill workloads -> Pattern 4 with managed batch endpoints or Airflow/Argo.


    You often compose two or three of these. For example, chat UX on Pattern 1, heavy tools offloaded to Pattern 3.
